\chapter{Me, and Two Ways to Part}
\label{ch:pa-me-and-parting}
\hlchaptermodality{35}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say to me with mainu and take my leave with changa ji or jaldi milaange, split mainu into the pronoun and the postposition fused inside it, hear the Persian ending shared by jaldi and khushi, and write mainu and the welcome from the previous chapter.}

The reader parts with a promise of soon, separates the borrowed adverb from the inherited verb, connects the Persian ending on jaldi to the one already met on khushi, runs three partings against each other, and writes mainu from memory using both marks traced in this chapter.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[mainū̃]{mainū̃ — the pronoun that changed shape}

\label{lesson:PA-C35-mainu}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{maiṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}I,\textquotedblright{} the pronoun you answer with. Say \emph{jī āiāṁ nū̃} from the last session, and listen for the small \emph{nū̃} on the end of it. Those two are about to meet.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\emph{mainū̃} — \textbf{me, to me}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Maiṁ} plus \emph{nū̃} does not come out as two words standing side by side. The pronoun bends first — \emph{maiṁ} becomes \emph{mai-} — and then the postposition fuses onto it: \emph{mainū̃}. Punjabi writes the result as one word.

English does something comparable and stops noticing it: \emph{I} becomes \emph{me} before a preposition, so nobody says \emph{to I}. Punjabi lets the seam show, because \emph{nū̃} is still recognisable inside the finished form.

The liking lesson handed you \emph{mainū̃ panjābī pasand hai} whole. It had to: the pieces had not been named. Now they have, and the same sentence can be rebuilt from parts — \emph{mainū̃} for the person who likes, \emph{panjābī} for the thing liked, \emph{pasand hai} for the liking.

That is why \emph{mainū̃} is a word and not merely a form. It is the shape \emph{maiṁ} takes whenever something is directed at the speaker, and it will return every time this book says something happens \textbf{to} someone.

On the page it needs two marks not yet traced — one below a letter, one above. Both are taught in this chapter.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mainū̃} — to me
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \emph{maiṁ} (I) and \emph{mainū̃} (to me)
  \item \emph{Rebuild:} \emph{mainū̃ panjābī pasand hai}, naming each piece as you place it
  \item \emph{State:} what happens to the pronoun before a postposition (it bends)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}to me.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Mainū̃}.) Which two pieces are inside it? (\emph{Maiṁ} and \emph{nū̃}.) Rebuild that liking sentence out of its parts.

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A8\%AE\%E0\%A9\%88\%E0\%A8\%A8\%E0\%A9\%82\%E0\%A9\%B0}{Wiktionary: mainu}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A8\%AE\%E0\%A9\%88\%E0\%A9\%B0}{Wiktionary: main}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[uu]{\pa{ੂ} — a mark that hangs underneath}

\label{lesson:PA-W09-dulainkar}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\pa{ਨ}} once. Then put the small tippi \textbf{\pa{ੰ}} above it, the way you did for \textbf{\pa{ਪੰਜਾਬੀ}}. Every vowel mark so far has sat on the line or above it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — one mark}
The \textbf{dulaiṅkaṛ} goes the other way. Trace \textbf{\pa{ਨੂ}} twice: write \textbf{\pa{ਨ}}, then hook the mark on underneath it, and say \emph{nū}. The vowel is a long \emph{ū}, the sound in English \emph{food}.

This is the second mark in this book to hang below a letter rather than above it. The \textbf{\pa{ਹ}} tucked under its neighbour in \emph{paṛhnā} was the first.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Cover the model. Write \textbf{\pa{ਨੂੰ}} once — letter, mark below, tippi above — then compare only whether the mark sits under the letter and not beside it.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
One mark, one direction: downward.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ai]{\pa{ੈ} — one stroke becomes two}

\label{lesson:PA-W09-dulavan}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\pa{ਤੇ}} once: the single slanting stroke above the line is the \emph{e} sign you met in \textbf{\pa{ਨਮਸਤੇ}}. Then write \textbf{\pa{ਨੂ}} from the session before, with its mark hanging below.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — one mark}
Double that slanting stroke and the vowel changes: \textbf{\pa{ੈ}}, the \textbf{dulāvāṁ}, sounds \emph{ai}. Trace \textbf{\pa{ਮੈ}} twice and say \emph{mai}.

Gurmukhi keeps a pattern here that is worth noticing on the page rather than being told about: one stroke above for \emph{e}, two for \emph{ai}; one hook below for \emph{u}, two for \emph{ū}. Counting strokes, not memorising shapes.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Cover the models. Write \textbf{\pa{ਤੇ}}, then \textbf{\pa{ਮੈ}}. Compare only the number of strokes above the line.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Two marks, counted rather than memorised.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[changā jī]{\pa{ਚੰਗਾ} \pa{ਜੀ} — a goodbye made of nothing new}

\label{lesson:PA-C35-changa-ji}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{changā}. Say \textbf{\pa{ਜੀ}}. Say \emph{mainū̃}. Three words from the last few sessions, none of them a farewell.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one phrase}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਚੰਗਾ} \pa{ਜੀ}} — \emph{changā jī} — \textbf{right then; bye}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\pa{ਚੰਗਾ}} was assembled two chapters ago; \textbf{\pa{ਜੀ}} has been writable since this run of chapters opened. Nothing here is a new shape: \textbf{\pa{ਚੰਗਾ} \pa{ਜੀ}}.

\begin{cousinweb}
This phrase adds no vocabulary. Its whole content is what happens when two known words are set in that order at the end of a conversation.

\emph{Changā} says good — the word whose trail stops at \emph{caṅga} and is argued no further. \textbf{\pa{ਜੀ}} adds the person. Together, at the door, they mean \emph{right then} — the exchange is agreed, so it can end.

The two farewells you learned first both promise. \emph{Phir milāṁge} promises another meeting; \emph{rabb rākhā} asks God to keep the other person. \emph{Changā jī} promises nothing. It closes by agreeing, which is why it fits a shopkeeper, a neighbour and a phone call, and why it is the parting a learner will hear most.

English does the same with \emph{all right then} and \emph{right you are}. A word for agreement, spoken at the end, becomes a way out.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Writing: assemble \pa{ਜੀ} \pa{ਆਇਆਂ} \pa{ਨੂੰ}}
The standalone long \emph{ā} and the hook that hangs below a letter have both been traced, so the welcome from the last chapter can be written out.

Three words. \textbf{\pa{ਜੀ}}. Then \textbf{\pa{ਆਇਆਂ}}: the standalone \textbf{\pa{ਆ}}, the standalone \textbf{\pa{ਇ}}, \textbf{\pa{ਆ}} again, and the dot \textbf{\pa{ਂ}} above. Then \textbf{\pa{ਨੂੰ}}: \textbf{\pa{ਨ}}, the hook below, the tippi above.

Copy the whole line once with the model visible. Cover it, write it again, and compare only the second word. Then add \textbf{\pa{ਸਲਾਮ}} and \textbf{\pa{ਠੀਕ}-\pa{ਠਾਕ}} underneath from memory, so neither goes cold.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{changā jī} — right then, bye
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \emph{phir milāṁge} (a promise) and \textbf{changā jī} (an agreement)
  \item \emph{Run through:} a tiny exchange — welcome someone in, then close with \textbf{changā jī}
  \item \emph{State:} how many new words this phrase taught (none)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Close a conversation. (\textbf{\pa{ਚੰਗਾ} \pa{ਜੀ}}.) What does each word mean on its own? (Good; respect.) Write the welcome from the last chapter once more.

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A8\%9A\%E0\%A9\%B0\%E0\%A8\%97\%E0\%A8\%BE}{Wiktionary: changa}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A8\%9C\%E0\%A9\%80}{Wiktionary: ji}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jaldī milāṁge]{\pa{ਜਲਦੀ} \pa{ਮਿਲਾਂਗੇ} — soon, borrowed; meet, inherited}

\label{lesson:PA-C35-jaldi-milaange}



\begin{quote}
Close a conversation with \textbf{\pa{ਚੰਗਾ} \pa{ਜੀ}}. Then recall \emph{khushī} from the introduction chapter, a Persian word wearing a Persian ending. Another one arrives now.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਜਲਦੀ}} — \emph{jaldī} — \textbf{soon, quickly}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\pa{ਜ}}, \textbf{\pa{ਲ}}, \textbf{\pa{ਦ}}, and the long \emph{ī} sign: \textbf{\pa{ਜਲਦੀ}}. The second word came from the farewell chapter and needed the looped letter and the throat letter this run has since taught: \textbf{\pa{ਮਿਲਾਂਗੇ}}. Both words are now writable in full: \textbf{\pa{ਜਲਦੀ} \pa{ਮਿਲਾਂਗੇ}}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\pa{ਜਲਦੀ}} rests on Persian \emph{jald}, \textquotedblleft{}quick, hurried\textquotedblright{} — a word Persian itself took from Arabic. On the end sits the Persian \emph{-ī}, which turns a quality into a noun or an adverb of that quality.

That ending is not new here. \emph{Khushī}, \textquotedblleft{}pleasure,\textquotedblright{} was \emph{khush}, \textquotedblleft{}happy,\textquotedblright{} carrying the same \emph{-ī}. Two words, one ending, the same job. A learner who notices the ending once can hear it inside dozens of Punjabi words, which is the kind of return an etymology has to pay to earn its place.

\textbf{\pa{ਮਿਲਾਂਗੇ}} is already yours from the farewells: \textquotedblleft{}we will meet.\textquotedblright{} Set the borrowed adverb in front of the inherited verb and the parting is complete — \emph{soon, we will meet}.

Note the order. Punjabi puts the verb at the end, as the introduction established with \emph{merā nāṁ ... hai}. English says \emph{see you soon} and finishes on the adverb; Punjabi opens on it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Writing: assemble \pa{ਮੈਨੂੰ}}
Both marks \emph{mainū̃} was waiting for have been traced. Build it: \textbf{\pa{ਮ}}, the two-stroke sign above it, \textbf{\pa{ਨ}}, the hook below, the tippi above. Written out: \textbf{\pa{ਮੈਨੂੰ}}.

Look at the model for a moment, then cover it and write the word from memory. Uncover, compare, and repair one thing only — whichever mark sits on the wrong side of the line. Then write \textbf{\pa{ਜੀ} \pa{ਆਇਆਂ} \pa{ਨੂੰ}} underneath: its last word ends in the same two marks you have placed.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{jaldī milāṁge} — see you soon
  \item \emph{State:} which half is borrowed and which is inherited
  \item \emph{Connect:} the ending on \textbf{\pa{ਜਲਦੀ}} to the ending on \emph{khushī}
  \item \emph{Run through:} three ways to part — \emph{phir milāṁge}, \textbf{changā jī}, \textbf{jaldī milāṁge}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Part with a promise of soon. (\textbf{\pa{ਜਲਦੀ} \pa{ਮਿਲਾਂਗੇ}}.) Which word is borrowed? (\textbf{\pa{ਜਲਦੀ}}.) Write \textbf{\pa{ਮੈਨੂੰ}} once from memory.

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A8\%9C\%E0\%A8\%B2\%E0\%A8\%A6\%E0\%A9\%80}{Wiktionary: jaldi}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D8\%AC\%D9\%84\%D8\%AF}{Wiktionary: jald}.
\end{tcolorbox}
